Behind the image

What is calculated, and what is drawn.

The model is the Schwarzschild solution of Einstein’s equations: the spacetime outside a non-rotating, uncharged, spherical mass. Lengths are in Schwarzschild radii (rₛ = 2GM/c²) and times in rₛ/c. For a black hole the mass of the Sun, rₛ ≈ 3 km and rₛ/c ≈ 10 μs.

Far-away time

The timeline is Schwarzschild coordinate time t: the time kept by an observer at rest very far away. Everything in the scene is shown at the same value of t.

Clocks A and B

Static clocks, held at fixed height (they need a rocket or a tower to stay put). Their own time τ runs at

dτ/dt = √(1 − rₛ/r)

Signals

Flashes travel radially from A to B along exact null paths, r + ln(r/rₛ − 1) = ±ct + const. Because the spacetime does not change with t, every flash takes the same coordinate time, so the spacing in B’s own time is stretched by √(1 − rₛ/rB) / √(1 − rₛ/rA). This is gravitational redshift: the same factor multiplies the wavelength, measured by clocks at rest at each height. Emitted light is set to 470 nm.

Light rays

Null geodesics integrated numerically (fourth-order Runge–Kutta, checked against the conserved null constraint and against the known deflection series). Rays with impact parameter below 3√3/2 rₛ are captured; the dark ray starts just above it and orbits near the photon sphere at 1.5 rₛ.

Falling clock C

Dropped from rest at radius R, it follows the exact radial geodesic r = R/2 (1 + cos η), τ = R3/2/2 (η + sin η). Its own time to reach the horizon is finite (22.4 rₛ/c from 6 rₛ), and to reach the centre only 0.7 more. In far-away time t it approaches the horizon forever and is never seen to cross.

Space view

The surface is Flamm’s paraboloid, z = 2√(rₛ(r − rₛ)): an exact, unexaggerated picture of the curved geometry of space around the mass, for one equatorial slice at one moment. Its depth shows extra distance, not time and not a rubber sheet pulled down by weight.

Time view

Two space dimensions plus coordinate time drawn upward. Ticks on each worldline are equal steps of that clock’s own time. Spatial curvature is not shown in this view; the transition between views is only a visual blend.

Touch and keys

Drag to orbit, pinch or scroll to zoom. In Time view, hover or tap a tick mark or a flash to see when and where it happened. Keys: Space play/pause, ← → step, T Space/Time, R replay.

Drawn for clarity rather than to scale: the clocks’ size and shape (each hand turns once per unit of that clock’s own time), the solid ball marking the horizon, the printed look of lines and dots, line brightness, the star background (not a real sky), and the colours of light (the redshift factor is exact; mapping a wavelength to a screen colour is approximate). Light rays are drawn on the spatial surface rather than as images a camera would see. Rotation (Kerr), charge and the inside of the horizon are not modelled.
